The cultural context of post-colonial India fundamentally shapes the expression of the theme of identity in the text by framing it as a dialectic rather than a static state. The setting, characterized by the tension between traditional Indian values and Western influences, transforms identity from an internal psychological journey into a sociopolitical negotiation. The "rapidly changing society" acts as an active agent that forces the younger generation to define themselves in opposition to or in synthesis with these conflicting forces. Consequently, the struggle for self is not merely about personal discovery but is deeply embedded in the historical legacy of colonialism and the immediate pressures of post-independence nation-building. This context elevates the theme of identity to a collective experience, where individual selfhood is inextricably linked to the broader cultural and historical shifts occurring around the family.
